title: DeCovarT reproducibility
text:
0.1 Aims
This book applies DeCovarT to the Suppinger murine gastruloid resource. It records what is run: the data, the algorithms as implemented, the hyperparameters and their values, the code, the outputs, and which outputs are stale. The reasons behind each choice are in the DeCovarT vignettes; each chapter links to the vignette section that states them and does not restate the theory.
The target is a covariance plug-in for the likelihood, not a biologically interpretable gene regulatory network (03-2, target). Indices follow the article: gene g=1,\ldots,G, type j=1,\ldots,J, bulk sample i=1,\ldots,N, cell c, with C_j cells of type j.

title: DeCovarT reproducibility
text:
Estimate, for each labelled cell type j at each bulk-matched time, the mean \widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} and the within-type covariance \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j} of a gene panel, on the linear scale that DeCovarT’s convolution needs. The source is one single-specimen scRNA-seq reference (GSE229513, Section 2.1).
Choose that panel for the purpose: genes whose moments can be estimated in every type and that carry information about the proportions \boldsymbol{p} (Section 3.1).
Plug the moments into DeCovarT and deconvolve the bulk series (GSE229386) where a single-cell reference matches it: the 48 h standard-Wnt samples.

title: DeCovarT reproducibility
text:
0.2 Pipeline
Figure 1 lists the nine steps in the order the scripts run them. Steps 2 to 5 are Section 3.1; step 7 is Section 4.1; step 8 is Section 5.1; step 9 is Section 6.1.






Figure 1: “Analysis pipeline, read left to right on each row. Row 1 builds the gene panel from the single-cell counts: quality control, a presence gate in every type, an omnibus count-model screen ranked by effect size, and a cross-platform filter fitted on the only matched pair (single-cell 48 h, standard-Wnt bulk 48 h). Row 2 estimates one covariance per type and time on the linear scale, with the tuning parameter of each estimator chosen by cross-validated held-out Gaussian log-likelihood, lifts the estimates to DeCovarT’s moments and deconvolves the matched bulk. The dashed box is optional; it needs the covariances of step 7.”



Branches that were tried and dropped are not drawn: ppcor partial correlations, the huge graphical lasso, penalty selection by EBIC alone, and exports on the log1p scale. ?sec-cov-stale lists the outputs those branches left behind.

title: 2  Suppinger gastruloids
text:
2.1 Hierarchical design
Single-cell UMI counts and bulk HTSeq tables come from the murine gastruloid resource of Suppinger and colleagues (Cell Stem Cell, 2023; GEO GSE229513 and GSE229386; (Suppinger et al. 2023)).
The scRNA-seq experiment is one 10x Chromium 3′ v3 resource from one specimen series, not a panel of independent biological replicates. DeCovarT treats it as the one-replicate regime (2.1, one single-cell replicate). Zeros are taken as molecule-sampling counts (Note 4.1). GSE250136 is a later stem-embryo dataset and is not part of this resource.
Figure 2.1 draws the two designs side by side.
Single-cell (GSE229513). The first factor is the mESC cell line (B-S or SBR), the second the time slot. Each line covers six slots, and only 48 h is profiled in both. At the three times of the bulk series the cell counts are (output/naive_marker_selection/tables/batch_by_time.csv):
Cell line is therefore confounded with time except at 48 h, and it is not a covariate in any fit of this book. The two lines are treated as one developmental trajectory (Figure 2.4). Gene ranking and covariance estimation run independently at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h, the slots with a bulk time point (Section 3.4, Section 4.1). At 48 h the two lines are pooled; Section 3.8 measures what pooling changes.
Bulk RNA-seq (GSE229386). The first factor is the Wnt schedule: the standard pulse at 48 h, or an early pulse at 24 h. The second factor is the time point, 48 h, 72 h or 96 h, each with three biological replicates. No single-cell slot carries the early schedule, so the early-Wnt bulk has no single-cell counterpart. The cross-platform filter of Section 3.7 is fitted on the matched pair only: single-cell 48 h against standard-Wnt bulk 48 h.

2.2 Seurat processing
Embeddings, QC and clustering follow the Seurat workflow of the Suppinger resource (Suppinger et al. 2023), drawn in Figure 2.2: Alevin counts, scater QC, SCTransform Pearson residuals per batch for integration, CCA, PCA, UMAP and Louvain clustering. Two products of that workflow are used here: the cell-type labels (celltypeannotation), and the gene list of the authors’ SCT counts layer, which serves as the gene allow-list (Section 3.2). The authors’ residuals themselves are not used: the ranking refits SCTransform v2 per time slot (Section 3.4), and the covariances are estimated from raw counts (Section 4.1.2).






Figure 2.2: Seurat workflow used to extract embeddings and downstream analyses on GSE229513.

title: 2  Suppinger gastruloids
text:
2.3 Biological interpretation from single-cell compositions
Figure 2.3 and Figure 2.4 summarise a putative reading of annotated type proportions along gastruloid time. They are not a reconstruction of embryonic lineages. Two annotated states are treated as technical artefacts of culture stress (Cd63+ ectoderm-like artefact and Zscan4+ artefact, data/dictionaries/suppinger_celltype_crosswalk.csv). The working caudal sequence after the Chir/Wnt pulse is pluripotency \to epiblast \to primitive streak \to caudal mesoderm / NMP \to pre-somitic mesoderm / somites, with a residual endoderm bias typical of gastruloids.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.1 Scope and status
This chapter builds the gene panel on which the covariances of Section 4.1 are estimated. It runs on the single-cell counts of GSE229513 at the three bulk-matched times (Section 2.1), one time at a time. What the panel must achieve, and why each step is there, is stated in the feature-selection vignette (3.1, estimand): genes whose type-level moments can be estimated in every type and that carry information about \boldsymbol{p}. The ranking statistics below are computed inside one specimen. They calibrate a screen, not a population-level claim of differential expression (Note 3.1).
Ranks are computed on SCTransform Pearson residuals or on a count GLM. Neither scale is exported: the moments that enter DeCovarT are on the linear scale (2.1, normalisation).
The current panel (top 500 per time, 1) comes from the between/within ratio. Once the presence gate, the omnibus rank and the bulk filter have been run, they replace that rank as steps 3 to 5 of Figure 1, and every output of Section 4.1 has to be refitted.

section: 3.2 Cell and gene QC as applied
text:
3.2 Cell and gene QC as applied
The tiers of quality control recommended in the vignette (3.1, QC) are applied only in part. What runs today is listed here.
Cells.

The authors’ Seurat QC (scater, Section 2.2) is taken as given.
01_01 keeps cells with a time slot in {48 h, 72 h, 96 h}, a non-missing celltypeannotation, and a library size above zero.
The culture-stress labels flagged include_in_ranking = FALSE in data/dictionaries/suppinger_celltype_crosswalk.csv (Cd63+ ectoderm-like artefact, Zscan4+ artefact) are dropped before the fit.
A type with fewer than min_cells = 20 cells in a slot stays in the SCTransform fit and is left out of the scores. Exiting naïve pluripotency at 72 h (8 cells) is the only such case.
No library-size MAD filter, detected-gene filter or mitochondrial filter is applied by this repository. This is the gap with tier (i) of the vignette.

Genes.

The allow-list is the gene set of the authors’ SCT counts layer: 2,944 of the 27,027 genes of the RNA assay. Genes outside it never enter a fit.
After the per-time fit, SCTransform returns residuals for 2,892 (48 h), 2,769 (72 h) and 2,811 (96 h) genes (model_card.csv).
Ribosomal, mitochondrial and sex-chromosome genes are not removed explicitly; whether the authors’ allow-list already excludes them has not been checked.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.3 Presence gate
A gene enters the ranking at a given time only if it is detected, and varies, in every scored type at that time. With \delta_{gj} the fraction of cells of type j with a non-zero count for gene g, and v_{gj} the within-type variance of the counts,

\min_{j}\delta_{gj}\ge\delta_{\min}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\min_{j}v_{gj}>0 .
\tag{3.1}
presence_gate() in R/rank_genes_omnibus.R returns the logical gene vector; \delta_{\min} is an argument fixed before the ranks are seen (the sketch below uses 0.05). The reasons for a gate in every type, rather than in at least one, are in 3.1, presence. In the current outputs the gate is absent. Its absence is one cause of the constant-gene fallback described in ?sec-cov-stale.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.4 SCTransform v2 fit per time
rank_genes_sctransform() refits Seurat::SCTransform() separately at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h (split_by = "time_point") on the allow-list genes. Cells of every non-artefact type at that time are fitted together. The fitted mean is an intercept plus a library-size offset,

\log\mu_{gc}
=
\beta_{0g}
+
\log s_{c},
\qquad
x_{gc}\sim\mathrm{NB}(\mu_{gc},\psi_{g}),
\tag{3.2}
with s_{c} the full RNA library size of cell c (column sum of the unfiltered count matrix, stored as log_umi =\log_{10}s_{c}), not the sum over the allow-list. The Pearson residual is r_{gc}=(x_{gc}-\hat\mu_{gc})/\sqrt{\hat\mu_{gc}+\hat\mu_{gc}^{2}/\hat\psi_{g}}.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.5 Current rank: between/within ratio
The residual matrix of one slot is split by type. With C_j cells of type j, \bar r_{gj} the mean residual of gene g in type j, and v_{gj} its within-type variance, the two decompositions are

\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between},g}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}C_{j}\bigl(\bar r_{gj}-\bar r_{g}\bigr)^{2},
\qquad
\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within},g}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}\sum_{c\in j}\bigl(r_{gc}-\bar r_{gj}\bigr)^{2}
\tag{3.3}
(every cell has weight one), and

\bar r_{g}^{\mathrm{eq}}
=
J^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\bar r_{gj},
\qquad
\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{between},g}
=
J^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J}(\bar r_{gj}-\bar r_{g}^{\mathrm{eq}})^{2},
\qquad
\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{within},g}
=
J^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J}v_{gj}
\tag{3.4}
(every type has weight 1/J). The score is the ratio of the between term to the within term. What this ratio estimates, and how it relates to a score test of the type effect, is in 3.1, consistency.
Three lists are built per slot (anova_ss(), anova_ms_equal_type(), rank_ratio()):

Global, equal cell weight. Top n_genes_global = 500 genes by \mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between}}/\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within}} (ranks_global.csv). The largest type dominates.
Global, equal type weight. Top 500 by \mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{between}}/\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{within}} (ranks_global_equal_type.csv). This list feeds the export of



Per cell type. One-versus-rest split, top n_genes_celltype = 50 genes by the equal-cell ratio (ranks_per_cell_type.csv). The flag \mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between}}>\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within}} is stored and not used as a gate: on unit-variance residuals it is an R^{2}>1/2 cut, which almost no gene meets when one type dominates the slot.

Each list is then united with the signalling markers of the types scored in that slot (Section 3.9).

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.6 Omnibus count-model rank
rank_genes_omnibus() (R/rank_genes_omnibus.R) replaces the residual ratio by a test of the cell-type main effect on the counts, then ranks the genes that pass by effect size. Per time slot, on the genes that pass the presence gate:

Fit the negative-binomial GLM \log\mu_{gc}=\beta_{0g}+\beta_{g,j(c)}+\log s_{c} with glmGamPoi::glm_gp(design = ~ cell_type, offset = log(s_c)) (Ahlmann-Eltze and Huber 2020). The offset is the full library size; size_factors is switched off so that it is not applied twice.
Test the joint type effect with glmGamPoi::test_de(fit, reduced_design = ~ 1): the quasi-likelihood F test of Lund et al. (2012) as implemented in glmGamPoi. The gate is a Benjamini–Hochberg threshold on adj_pval.
Rank the genes that pass by an effect size, the deviance explained R^{2}_{D,g}=1-\mathcal{D}_g(M_1)/\mathcal{D}_g(M_0), with the types weighted equally as in Equation 3.4.


# Not run. counts: genes x cells of one slot; cell_type: factor over
# cells; lib: full library sizes (10^log_umi). Thresholds are set
# before the ranks are seen.
source("R/rank_genes_omnibus.R")
keep <- presence_gate(counts, cell_type, min_detection = 0.05)
ranked <- rank_genes_omnibus(counts[keep, ], cell_type, library_size = lib)

# The two glmGamPoi calls it wraps:
fit <- glmGamPoi::glm_gp(
  counts[keep, ],
  design = ~cell_type,
  col_data = data.frame(cell_type = cell_type),
  offset = log(lib),
  size_factors = FALSE
)
qlf <- glmGamPoi::test_de(fit, reduced_design = ~1)

The wrapper arguments in the chunk are illustrative; the definitive signatures are those of R/rank_genes_omnibus.R. Why a gate followed by an effect size, rather than a rank by p-value, is in 3.1, omnibus.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.7 48 h bulk consistency filter
bulk_consistency_filter() (R/bulk_consistency.R) removes genes whose bulk expression cannot be produced by the single-cell reference. It needs a single-cell slot and a bulk sample of the same condition. In Suppinger the only such pair is single-cell 48 h (B-S and SBR pooled) against the standard-Wnt bulk at 48 h, three biological replicates (Figure 2.1). The early-Wnt bulk has no matched reference.

Fit. At 48 h only: for each gene, compare the bulk value of each replicate with the range that the 48 h type means allow, and flag median-absolute-deviation outliers. The thresholds follow RNA-Sieve’s range bound and outlier rule as described in the vignette.
Apply. The flagged genes are removed from the panel at every time, including 72 h and 96 h, where no matched pair exists.
Status. A heuristic, labelled as such in the code. No script reads the bulk HTSeq table yet (01_01 does not); the filter has not been run.

The model behind the bound, and the alternatives that keep such genes and down-weight them, are in 3.1, cross-platform.

# Not run. sc48: counts of the 48 h slot with labels; bulk48: the three
# standard-Wnt 48 h replicates from GSE229386, same gene identifiers.
source("R/bulk_consistency.R")
flags <- bulk_consistency_filter(sc48, cell_type48, bulk48)
panel <- setdiff(panel, flags$gene[flags$flagged])

text:
3.8 Cell-line sensitivity at 48 h
48 h is the only slot that contains both cell lines. The script output/naive_marker_selection/cell_line_48h/01_03_sensitivity_48h_cell_line.R refits the same v2 model inside B-S and inside SBR and compares the equal-cell top 500 and the per-type top 50. (It lives under output/ next to its results; scripts/01_03_export_equal_type_seurat.R is a different script.)

The two global lists share 308 of 500 genes (Jaccard 0.45).
Epiblast shares 29, and exiting naïve pluripotency 30, of its top 50.
Naïve pluripotency is scored in SBR only: B-S has fewer than 20 cells of that type.

Outputs: overlap_48h_cell_line.csv, ranks_global_48h_by_line.csv, ranks_per_cell_type_48h_by_line.csv, venn_48h_cell_line.pdf.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.9 Knowledge-driven markers
The marker list is curated and short: data/dictionaries/mouse_gastruloid_signaling_markers.csv, with columns cell_type_excel (lineage on the signalling map), cell_type_suppinger (the matching Suppinger label, or NA) and gene_marker. Symbols are mapped offline with org.Mm.eg.db (R/map_marker_symbols.R), not biomaRt.
Fifteen of the 19 mouse symbols are in the 2,944-gene allow-list. Under a uniform draw of 19 genes from the 27,027 RNA symbols the expected overlap is about 2.1; the hypergeometric upper tail is P(X\ge 15)=8.8\times10^{-12} (marker_sct_hypergeometric.csv). The four absent markers are Myod1, Pax6, Sox1 and Tfap2a (venn_markers_vs_counts.pdf).

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.11 Optional multivariate refinement
A univariate rank ignores redundancy between genes and the covariances DeCovarT models. The optional stage searches subsets of the panel with a multi-objective criterion on all types jointly (3.1, multivariate). It needs \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}, so it runs after Section 4.1, and it is drawn dashed in Figure 1.
Planned settings:

Optimiser. NSGA-II through mco::nsga2() (Mersmann et al. 2020). Genes are encoded as a mask in [0,1]^{G}, thresholded to a target panel size.
Objectives, all minimised:

the 2-norm condition number \kappa_{2}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\mathcal{G}}) of the mean signature restricted to the panel;
the mean pairwise MixSim overlap of the J Gaussians \mathcal{N}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}) (Melnykov et al. 2012, 2021);
optionally, minus the smallest eigenvalue of the Fisher information for \boldsymbol{p}, as a sensitivity objective on a shortlist of non-dominated panels.

Output. The whole Pareto front, not one panel. With one specimen, any panel chosen here is fitted on this atlas and has to be challenged on an external gastruloid cohort.

scripts/04_02_feature_selection_genetic_algorithm.R is a template: it stops with an error until the fitness function is implemented on a real panel.

  g <- which(mask > 0.5)
  kappa2 <- kappa(mu[g, , drop = FALSE], exact = TRUE)
  ov <- MixSim::overlap(
    Pi = rep(1 / J, J),
    Mu = t(mu[g, , drop = FALSE]),
    S = simplify2array(lapply(Sigma, \(A) A[g, g, drop = FALSE]))
  )
  c(kappa2, mean(ov$OmegaMap[upper.tri(ov$OmegaMap)]))
}
front <- mco::nsga2(fitness, idim = nrow(mu), odim = 2L,

3.12 What is not run






Warning 3.1: ⚠️ Cells of one specimen are not biological replicates



GSE229513 has one specimen series. Cells, or random partitions of cells, are technical draws; resampling them measures sampling variability inside the specimen, not variability between organoids (Squair et al. 2021; Zimmerman et al. 2021). No calibrated differential-expression claim is made in this book. The bulk series GSE229386 does have three biological replicates per time and schedule; they support bulk contrasts, not single-cell ones.


The following were considered and are not part of the pipeline. Each is reviewed in 3.1, review.

Pseudo-bulk DESeq2, edgeR or limma–voom: no biological replicates at the level of the contrast (Note 3.1).
MAST hurdle tests: droplet UMI counts are modelled without a zero-inflation layer (Note 4.1).
Differential-network screens (INDEED, D-trace) and Markov-boundary growth of marker seeds: they need fitted graphs and belong to the perspectives of the covariance vignette (3.3, perspectives).

4.1 Scope and status
This chapter estimates, for each scored cell type j at each bulk-matched time, the mean \widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} and the within-type covariance \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} of the gene panel of Section 3.10, and exports them on the linear scale of DeCovarT’s convolution,
\bigl\{
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j},\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}^{-1}
\bigr\}_{j=1}^{J},
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}\succ 0 .
\tag{4.1}
The target is the covariance that enters the likelihood, not a mechanistic gene network; a dense estimate is therefore an acceptable plug-in and is the default (3.2, target).
Nothing in this chapter has produced a usable covariance yet. The outputs that exist are stale and are kept only as a record of what went wrong (?sec-cov-stale).

4.2.1 Shrinkage covariance (default)
fit_cov_shrinkage() calls corpcor::cov.shrink() (Schäfer et al. 2021) with the Schäfer–Strimmer target D: variances kept, correlations shrunk towards zero by a common factor (Schäfer and Strimmer 2005). corpcor 1.6.10 also shrinks the variances towards their median by default; lambda.var = 0 switches that off, so the target is exactly D. The closed-form intensity \hat\lambda^{\ast} (corpcor::estimate.lambda()) is the centre of the grid, and cross-validation picks the value used. The estimate is positive definite for any C_j and G, so it is the estimator used when the others fail. The theory is in 3.2, shrinkage. corpcor is not in renv.lock.


4.2.2 Graphical lasso with an unpenalised diagonal
fit_cov_glasso() standardises the panel, fits glasso::glasso(R, rho = lambda, penalize.diagonal = FALSE) (Friedman et al. 2019) on the sample correlation \boldsymbol{R}_j by block coordinate descent (Friedman et al. 2008), and rescales: \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}=\Delta_j^{-1/2}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{R}\Delta_j^{-1/2} with \Delta_j=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{V}_j) (rescale_correlation_fit()). With the diagonal unpenalised the fitted correlation keeps a unit diagonal, so \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} matches the sample variances.

penalize.diagonal defaults to TRUE in glasso 1.11; it is set explicitly.
huge (Zhao et al. 2022) is not used: huge.glasso() always penalises the diagonal and has no switch for it (checked in the huge 1.5.1 sources). The reasons are in 3.3, graphical lasso.
Grid endpoints come from lambda_endpoints(): at \lambda_{\max}=\max_{g\neq g'}|R_{gg'}| the off-diagonal precision is zero; the lower end is of order \sqrt{\log G/C_j}.
A gene constant across the cells of a type is left out of that type’s fit and listed in excluded_genes, instead of forcing a diagonal covariance for all genes.
A penalty whose solve fails is dropped from the grid and listed in failed_lambda, instead of being replaced by a diagonal precision.

The earlier selector, a safeguarded EBIC interval search (ebic_adaptive_path(), at most n_solves = 40 solves, \gamma=0.5 (Foygel and Drton 2010)), is kept in scripts/03_01_grn_huge.R as a diagnostic path. It no longer chooses \lambda.

SILGGM::SILGGM(npn, method = "D-S_GL", global = TRUE, alpha) (Zhang et al. 2018b, 2018a): de-sparsified graphical lasso with the global FDR rule of

The object kept is the support at level \alpha (global_decision), not the dense de-sparsified matrix.

An SPD refit on the linear-scale panel under the zeros of that support, with glasso::glasso(V, rho = 0, zero = ..., penalize.diagonal = FALSE).

The script scripts/03_02_grn_silggm.R (seed 1, \alpha=0.05) stops after step 2 and has never been run; the refit lives in the wrapper.

fit_cov_plnnetwork() fits the Poisson-lognormal network of PLNmodels (Chiquet et al. 2025, 2018) to the raw counts of one unit, with the full-library offset:

\begin{algorithm} \caption{PLNnetwork: alternating graphical lasso and variational updates} \begin{algorithmic} \Require counts $X$, offsets $O=\log s$, penalty $\lambda$, weights $W$ \State initialise the variational means $M$, variances $S$ and $\Sigma$ \For{$h = 1,\ldots,$ maxit\_out} \State $\Omega^{(h)} \gets$ \Call{GraphicalLasso}{$\Sigma^{(h-1)}, \lambda W$} \State $(B^{(h)},M^{(h)},S^{(h)}) \gets$ \Call{NLopt}{$B^{(h-1)},M^{(h-1)},S^{(h-1)};\Omega^{(h)}$} \State $\Sigma^{(h)} \gets C^{-1}\left[{M^{(h)}}^\top M^{(h)} + \sum_c S_c^{(h)}\right]$ \State $F_h \gets -\mathrm{ELBO}(B^{(h)},M^{(h)},S^{(h)},\Omega^{(h)}) + \lambda\|\Omega^{(h)}\|_{1,W}$ \If{$|F_h-F_{h-1}|/|F_h| <$ ftol\_out} \State \textbf{break} \EndIf \EndFor \State \Return $(B,M,S,\Omega,\Sigma)$ \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}


Algorithm 4.1 is the block-coordinate scheme of Chiquet et al. (2018). The model, the variational bound and the role of the offset are in 3.3, PLN.
The latent moments (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{z},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}) are not on DeCovarT’s scale. pln_linear_moments() maps them to the moments of the counts, averaged over the size factors s_c of the cells being scored:

\mathbb{E}\,x_{gc}=s_{c}\,e^{\mu_{z,g}+\sigma_{z,gg}/2},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}
=
\operatorname{diag}(\mathbb{E}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c})
+
\bigl(\mathbb{E}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}\,\mathbb{E}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}^{\top}\bigr)
\circ
\bigl(e^{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}}-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\bigr),
\tag{4.3}
with e^{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}} taken entrywise. The moments are then divided by the size factor, so that the four estimators are scored on the same size-factor-normalised table.

title: 4  Covariance estimation
text:
4.3 Cross-validation and outputs
The same loss selects the tuning parameter of every estimator and compares the four: the held-out Gaussian log-likelihood on the linear scale. For held-out cells \mathcal{T} and an estimate (\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}) fitted without them,

\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}};\mathcal{T})
=
\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{T}}
\log\phi_{G}\bigl(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c};\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\bigr),
\tag{4.4}
computed by heldout_gaussian_logscore() through a Cholesky factor of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}. Why this score is a legitimate loss for the covariance even though cells are not Gaussian, and why it replaces AIC, BIC and EBIC as the selector, is in 3.2, cross-validation.


\begin{algorithm} \caption{Tuning by K-fold cross-validation, and nested comparison of the four estimators} \begin{algorithmic} \Procedure{CVSelect}{$X, f, \Lambda, K$} \State split the cells of $X$ into $K$ folds at random, with a fixed seed \For{$\lambda \in \Lambda$} \For{$k = 1,\ldots,K$} \State $(\hat\mu,\hat\Sigma) \gets f(X_{-k};\lambda)$ \State $\ell_k(\lambda) \gets$ \Call{HeldOutLogScore}{$\hat\mu,\hat\Sigma,X_k$} \EndFor \State $m(\lambda) \gets$ mean of $\ell_k(\lambda)$; $\mathrm{se}(\lambda) \gets$ its standard error \EndFor \State $\lambda_{\min} \gets \arg\max_{\lambda} m(\lambda)$ \State $\lambda_{1\mathrm{se}} \gets$ most regularised $\lambda$ with $m(\lambda) \ge m(\lambda_{\min}) - \mathrm{se}(\lambda_{\min})$ \State \Return $(m, \mathrm{se}, \lambda_{\min}, \lambda_{1\mathrm{se}})$ \EndProcedure \Procedure{NestedCompare}{$X, \{(f_e,\Lambda_e)\}_{e=1}^{4}, K_{\mathrm{out}}, K_{\mathrm{in}}$} \For{$k = 1,\ldots,K_{\mathrm{out}}$} \For{$e = 1,\ldots,4$} \State $\lambda_e \gets \lambda_{\min}$ of \Call{CVSelect}{$X_{-k}, f_e, \Lambda_e, K_{\mathrm{in}}$} \State $(\hat\mu,\hat\Sigma) \gets f_e(X_{-k};\lambda_e)$ \State $s_{ek} \gets$ \Call{HeldOutLogScore}{$\hat\mu,\hat\Sigma,X_k$} \EndFor \EndFor \State \Return $(s_{ek})$, paired by outer fold \EndProcedure \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}


Settings in scripts/03_04_cv_covariance.R:

cv_select_tuning(X, fit_fun, grid, K = 5, seed) returns the mean and standard error per grid value and the min and 1se choices. The exported fit uses min; 1se is reported beside it.
nested_cv_compare(X, estimators, K_outer = 5, K_inner = 5, seed) is run only to compare the four estimators. The inner loop chooses the tuning parameter, the outer loop scores the chosen fit on cells it never saw.
Folds split cells of one unit. The score measures generalisation to new cells of this specimen, not to new specimens (Note 3.1).
In units with very few cells (29 cells for the somite differentiation front) each training fold has about 23 cells; the shrinkage estimate is the only one expected to be stable there.

Diagnostics that are computed but do not select: the EBIC path of the graphical lasso (Section 4.2.2), and edge stability under subsampling. StARS is not run: with 20 subsamples and 40 penalties it costs about 800 graphical-lasso solves per unit, against 40 for the EBIC path.

For the estimator retained for a unit, \widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} is the mean of the size-factor-normalised counts of its cells and \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} is the selected covariance, both on the scale of Section 4.1.2; Equation 4.1 holds by construction. For PLNnetwork both come from Equation 4.3. The lift from these cell-level moments to the population Gaussian that the convolution uses is Section 5.1.


4.3.1 Displays
Plot functions are in R/plot_grn_regularisation.R. Each display answers one question.
Choosing the tuning parameter (one unit, one estimator).

Cross-validation curve: m(\lambda)\pm\mathrm{se}(\lambda) against the tuning parameter, with the min and 1se choices marked (new; not produced yet).
Regularisation path: each off-diagonal entry of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}(\lambda) against \log\lambda, five edges that survive at the selected \lambda and five that are driven to zero (graphical lasso, PLNnetwork).
EBIC against \log\lambda, and EBIC against edge density |E|/\{G(G-1)/2\} (diagnostic only).

Comparing estimators (one unit).

Outer-fold held-out scores s_{ek} of Algorithm 4.2, one line per fold across the four estimators, so that the comparison is paired.
Partial-correlation heatmaps at the selected tuning parameter, with one gene order frozen across estimators and types, 
\rho_{gg'\mid\mathrm{rest}}
=
-\frac{\omega_{gg'}}{\sqrt{\omega_{gg}\omega_{g'g'}}},
\tag{4.5} on a diverging scale centred at zero.
For the three sparse estimators: UpSet plots of edge presence and of signed edges.

Comparing types (one time). Pairwise Hellinger distance and MixSim overlap between the exported Gaussians on the linear scale (gaussian_hellinger(), gaussian_mixsim_overlap() in R/ebic_regularisation_path.R). Distances computed on another scale (nonparanormal scores, \log(1+x)) do not describe what DeCovarT has to separate.


4.3.2 Evaluation
There is no ground-truth network for murine gastruloids, and the estimand is a covariance. The scores are therefore relative, in this order of weight:

Held-out likelihood, outer folds of Algorithm 4.2: the selector, and the only score that compares all four estimators on one scale.
Downstream deconvolution: DeCovarT error on the matched 48 h bulk and in the misspecification sweep of Section 8.1, with \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} from each estimator. This is the score tied to the paper’s estimand.
Technical stability: a bootstrap of cells within type, labels fixed (Section 5.4). Edge-inclusion frequencies for the sparse estimators and the Frobenius spread of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} for all four. Conditional on this specimen.
Separation of types: Hellinger and MixSim overlap of



Concordance of the sparse estimators: overlap of edge sets (intersection over the smaller set) and Hamming distance between skeletons, raw and divided by G(G-1)/2. Agreement is a robustness number, not a validation.

Scores that need a known skeleton, curated transcription-factor targets, other assays or perturbations are perspectives (3.3, perspectives).






Note 4.1: ℹ️ No zero-inflation layer



Suppinger is droplet UMI data. Zeros are modelled as Poisson or negative-binomial sampling zeros (Svensson 2020); no estimator in this book has a zero-inflation or hurdle layer. Zero-inflated observation models appear only as a contamination in Section 8.1.

title: 5  From single cells to type-level Gaussians
text:
5.1 Alignment of type-level Gaussians
DeCovarT does not ingest single-cell profiles. It needs, for each labelled type j, a population-level Gaussian (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}) whose precision is sparse. This chapter is about lifting cell-level observations to that object, and about checking that the lift still represents the cells.
Two strategies are in the core. Optimal transport and mechanistic simulators are perspectives (Section 5.7.1).
crumbs: 5  From single cells to type-level Gaussians

title: 5  From single cells to type-level Gaussians
text:
Affine invariance. Closed-form means and covariances when cells of one type are independent Gaussians.
Resampling. A technical bootstrap of cells, and Monte Carlo from scDesign3, with negative-binomial GAMLSS margins and a Gaussian copula tied to the sparse precision (Section 5.5). Figure 5.1 summarises the two routes.







Figure 5.1: Core lifts from labelled cells of one type to a population Gaussian: an affine aggregation, and resampling (bootstrap or scDesign3). The bulk profile is a later convolution across types.









Figure 5.2: Complementary schematic of the same sparse-copula arm, drawn for the one-cell-type scDesign2 case: negative-binomial margins per labelled type, a Gaussian copula whose correlation comes from the sparse precision, then synthetic counts with the observed cell-type proportions and library sizes. The TikZ diagram above is the reference layout; this figure gives the fitting and generating steps in more detail.









Warning 5.1: ⚠️ A within-type sum is not the bulk convolution



Write \boldsymbol{x}_{c\cdot j} for cell c of type j. The object of this chapter is a sum inside one type,

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\cdot j}
=
\sum_{c\in C_{j}} w_{c}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{c\cdot j},
\tag{5.1}
with \sum_{c}w_{c}=1 or w_{c}\equiv 1. Independent cells add means and add covariances with weights w_{c}^{2}. That sum estimates \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j} and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}.
The DeCovarT observation is a convolution across types,

\boldsymbol{y}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J} p_{j}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j}^{\mathrm{pop}},
\qquad
\mathrm{Cov}(\boldsymbol{y})
=
\sum_{j}p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}.
\tag{5.2}
The factor p_{j}^{2} belongs to that convolution. This chapter compares \{\boldsymbol{x}_{c\cdot j}\}_{c\in C_{j}} with \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}).

title: 5  From single cells to type-level Gaussians
text:
5.2 Which covariance to export
DeCovarT today is a Gaussian convolution of one population profile per type. The covariance weight is quadratic in the cell fraction. That object is a between-replicate phenotype, not the scatter of cells inside one donor. The three layers are drawn in Figure 5.3. MuSiC’s library-size assumptions, including the extra A3' hypothesis needed for absolute cell fractions, are in Figure 5.4.






Figure 5.3: Within-sample cell noise, between-replicate biological covariance, and residual bulk noise.









Figure 5.4: MuSiC assumptions for library-size normalisation: same population, conserved cell-size ratios, conserved library-size ratios, and the stronger A3-prime hypothesis for absolute cell-type fractions.



Before droplet scRNA-seq, the reference was a FACS- or MACS-purified bulk library. Szaniszlo et al. showed that mixture expression reflects composition, that a minor subset is recovered only after physical sorting, and that coexpression among genes inside a purified type is already a population-level object (Szaniszlo et al. 2004). Novershtern et al. profiled 38 marker-defined haematopoietic populations and used coexpression modules plus promoter cis-circuits as the gene–gene structure of each state (Novershtern et al. 2011). Those FACS profiles still match DeCovarT’s quadratic convolution.
Cells from one donor share genetic and environmental background, so they are subsamples rather than independent biological units (Zimmerman et al. 2021). Zimmerman, Espeland and Langefeld document that dependence across cell types, contrast within-donor cell variation with between-donor biological variation, and treat donor as the random effect when comparing conditions. That within-versus-between split is the same hierarchy as \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j} versus \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j} when a single-cell reference is aligned with bulk. Technical library-size and platform scale sit in a third, residual layer (Figure 5.4). Squair et al. make the same point for false discoveries if cells are treated as biological replicates (Squair et al. 2021).
The package outlook DeCovarT single-cell reference moments derives the moments. The practical fork on this gastruloid is the reference design.

5.2.1 One biological replicate
Identify the per-cell mean by the arithmetic mean of raw counts, and the within-cell covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}. Do not identify a between-replicate covariance: one donor is one draw of the replicate effect, and more cells only shrink the average of the cell noise.
Use a linear mixture covariance

\kappa_i\sum_j p_{ji}\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}
+
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{obs},i},
\tag{5.3}
with \kappa_i an effective inverse cell count for the bulk, and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{obs},i} diagonal. Keep a quadratic term only for the Monte Carlo error of the reference mean, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}/C_{j1}, and label it as such.
Report RNA fractions unless the transcriptome sizes S_j are measured. If they are measured, insert them in the mean. Do not estimate them jointly with \boldsymbol{p}, and do not estimate a gene-wise platform vector on the same bulk sample (Figure 5.4).


5.2.2 Enough biological replicates
R\ge 2 is the smallest design that identifies a variance component, by contrasting the covariance of replicate means with \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}/C_{jr}. An unstructured gene-by-gene between-replicate covariance is not estimable at transcriptome scale for the replicate counts of a normal single-cell study. Estimate a sparse or low-rank precision for \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j}. MEAD states the same small-R constraint on scRNA-seq references (Xie and Wang 2023).
The bulk model is then the three-layer normal likelihood

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}]
&=
a_i\sum_j p_{ji}\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\\
\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i})
&=
\sum_j p_{ji}^{2}\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j}
+
\kappa_i\sum_j p_{ji}\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}
+
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{obs},i}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.4}
a_i is one positive scale per bulk sample. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{obs},i} stays diagonal because gene–gene correlation already sits in the two biological layers.
Summing cells remains the right pseudobulk for DESeq2-style differential expression of one cell type across donors (Love et al. 2014). It is the wrong signature column, because the capture count would enter \boldsymbol{p}.
Second-generation engines already implement pieces of this split. MuSiC and MuSiC2 weight genes by cross-subject versus cross-cell consistency (Wang et al. 2019; Fan et al. 2022). DWLS averages cells for the mean and sums them to simulate bulk (Tsoucas et al. 2019). Bisque learns a gene-wise platform map from paired assays (Jew et al. 2020). RNA-Sieve and MEAD treat the reference as an errors-in-variables design (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021; Xie and Wang 2023). DECALS estimates a subject-specific bulk covariance and returns asymptotic intervals (Cai et al. 2024). RCTD is the spatial analogue for platform-corrected reference uncertainty (Cable et al. 2022). ReDeconv keeps transcriptome size in the reference (Lu et al. 2025).

text:
5.5 scDesign3 with a precision-based copula
scDesign3 fits a joint count model to cells, then draws synthetic cells from it (Song et al. 2024). Each gene gets its own margin, a generalised additive model for location, scale and shape (GAMLSS) in the cell covariates. A copula then joins the genes, which keeps the margins fixed while modelling pairwise dependence. The likelihood splits into a marginal part and a copula part, so AIC and BIC can score each part separately. With cell type as the only cell covariate, the model reduces to scDesign2, which fits one margin per gene and type and an empirical Gaussian copula per type (Sun et al. 2021).
The arm used here keeps that layout and changes the dependence: margins are negative binomial, and the copula correlation is the correlation matrix of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}^{-1} (Figure 5.5). Figure 5.2 shows the same sparse-copula arm in its scDesign2 form, with the fitting and generating steps spelled out.






Noteℹ️ Out of scope



scDesign3 also simulates continuous trajectories (pseudotime smoothers), spatial transcriptomics (Gaussian-process smoothers on coordinates) and multi-omic or multimodal profiles. DeCovarT is a static model of labelled cell types, so this chapter uses only the cell-type covariate, the GAMLSS margins, the copula and the likelihood-based model selection.








Figure 5.5: The scDesign3 arm used here, in plate notation. (a) Negative-binomial GAMLSS margins fitted gene by gene, with mean and dispersion depending on the labelled cell type and the mean offset by the library size. (b) A Gaussian copula whose correlation \boldsymbol{R}_j is the correlation matrix of the exported sparse covariance \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j^{-1}; the latent normal vector is mapped to uniforms and then through the inverse margins of (a).




5.5.1 Margins: a GAMLSS per gene
In scDesign3 notation, cell i has state covariates \boldsymbol{x}_i (cell type, pseudotime or coordinates) and design covariates \boldsymbol{z}_i=(b_i,c_i) (batch and condition). Feature j follows a distribution F_j whose mean, scale and zero-inflation parameters each have their own additive predictor (equation 1 of the paper):

\begin{aligned}
Y_{ij}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{z}_i
&\overset{\text{ind}}{\sim}F_j(\cdot\mid\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{z}_i;\mu_{ij},\sigma_{ij},p_{ij}),\\
\theta_j(\mu_{ij})&=\alpha_{j0}+\alpha_{jb_i}+\alpha_{jc_i}+f_{jc_i}(\boldsymbol{x}_i),\\
\log\sigma_{ij}&=\beta_{j0}+\beta_{jb_i}+\beta_{jc_i}+g_{jc_i}(\boldsymbol{x}_i),\\
\operatorname{logit}p_{ij}&=\gamma_{j0}+\gamma_{jb_i}+\gamma_{jc_i}+h_{jc_i}(\boldsymbol{x}_i).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.10}
\theta_j is the link of the mean. F_j is one of Gaussian, Bernoulli, Poisson, negative binomial, zero-inflated Poisson or zero-inflated negative binomial. When only \mu_{ij} depends on the covariates, Equation 5.10 is a generalised additive model (GAM); the GAMLSS adds predictors for the scale and the zero-inflation. The fit is gamlss() from gamlss or gam() from mgcv (Song et al. 2024).
The smooth terms f,g,h are what make the model additive: cubic regression splines along pseudotime, or Gaussian-process smoothers on spatial coordinates. For a categorical cell type x_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\} they collapse to one coefficient per type, f_{jc_i}(x_i)=\alpha_{jc_ix_i}. In this chapter’s notation (cell c, gene g, type j(c), library size L_c), the arm fits

X_{cg}\sim\mathrm{NB}(\mu_{cg},\psi_{cg}),
\qquad
\log\mu_{cg}=\alpha_{g0}+\alpha_{g\,j(c)}+\log L_c,
\qquad
\log\psi_{cg}=\beta_{g0}+\beta_{g\,j(c)},
\tag{5.11}
which is the per-type negative binomial of scDesign2 written as a GAMLSS: \mu_{gj} and \psi_{gj} are free per type, and the dispersion is allowed to differ between types. The library size enters the mean as an offset; replacing the offset by a covariate with a free slope is an ordinary GAMLSS term and tests whether expression scales proportionally with depth. Zero-inflated margins are not used (Note 4.1).
GAMLSS terms that do matter for DeCovarT, even without trajectories:

Dispersion by type. The negative-binomial dispersion is a scale parameter. Letting \log\psi depend on the type is the GAMLSS feature that a GAM lacks.
Design covariates. Batches or sampling time points enter as \alpha_{gb} and \beta_{gb}. Setting those coefficients to zero at generation produces synthetic cells without the batch effect.
Smooth terms. These are only needed when a continuous covariate is modelled, such as developmental time inside one labelled type. That is a perspective here, because DeCovarT’s reference is static.



5.5.2 Joint law: copula choices with fixed margins
The joint distribution factors by Sklar’s theorem (Theorem 5.1): the gene-wise cdfs F_{cg} carry the margins, and a copula C carries the dependence,

F(\boldsymbol{x}_{c}\mid j(c))
=C\bigl(F_{c1}(x_{c1}),\ldots,F_{cG}(x_{cG})\mid j(c)\bigr).

Because the margins are fitted first and held fixed, the copula changes only the pairwise dependence. Three copulas are available.



Table 5.1: Copulas that keep negative-binomial margins fixed and model pairwise gene dependence. \lvert E_j\rvert is the number of edges of the sparse precision of type j.











Copula
Dependence parameters per type

What it shows

Fails when G>n_j: \widehat{\boldsymbol{R}}_j is singular
A correlation matrix


Vine (scDesign3)
One bivariate copula per edge of G-1 trees
Always defined; slow
The first tree: genes that act as hubs


Precision-based Gaussian (this arm)
\lvert E_j\rvert non-zero partial correlations
Always defined: \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j\succ 0

Empirical Gaussian copula. scDesign3 estimates \boldsymbol{R}(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{z}_i) as the sample correlation of \Phi^{-1}(\boldsymbol{u}) among cells with the same covariates (cora() in Rfast). The authors note that when the number of genes is large, \widehat{\boldsymbol{R}} is not invertible and the likelihood cannot be computed (Song et al. 2024).
Vine copula. A regular vine decomposes the G-dimensional copula density into bivariate copulas along a sequence of G-1 trees, each conditioning on the previous ones (vinecop() in rvinecopulib). The density is always defined. The first tree is interpretable: in peripheral blood cells, it recovered canonical markers such as LYZ for CD14^{+} monocytes and CD79A for B cells as hub genes. Fitting is slow in high dimension (Song et al. 2024).
Precision-based Gaussian copula. This arm does not estimate the copula from the counts. The latent map z_{cg}=\Phi^{-1}(u_{cg}) is the same idea as huge.npn() followed by a Gaussian precision (3.3, graphical lasso, Section 4.2.3, 3.3, nonparanormal): monotone margins, then a Gaussian vector. SILGGM estimates the precision of those scores. Here the precision is the exported \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}, and the copula is not refit. The correlation that enters the copula is

R_{gg'}
=
\frac{\Sigma_{gg'}}{\sqrt{\Sigma_{gg}\,\Sigma_{g'g'}}},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
=
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}^{-1}.
\tag{5.12}
R is the correlation of that covariance. It is not the matrix of partial correlations, and it is not the Pearson correlation of the raw counts. Its inverse is \boldsymbol{R}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{D}^{1/2}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j\boldsymbol{D}^{1/2} with \boldsymbol{D}=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}), so the zero pattern of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j survives: two genes with a zero partial correlation are conditionally independent on the latent normal scale. The copula matches the network only if \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j was estimated on the normal scores, as SILGGM does after the nonparanormal map; a precision estimated on linear counts gives a correlation on another scale.

Theorem 5.1 (Sklar’s theorem) Let F be a G-dimensional cdf with margins F_{1},\ldots,F_{G}. There exists a copula C:[0,1]^{G}\to[0,1] such that

F(x_{1},\ldots,x_{G})
=
C\bigl(F_{1}(x_{1}),\ldots,F_{G}(x_{G})\bigr).
\tag{5.13}
If every F_{g} is continuous, C is unique. If some margins are discrete, C is uniquely determined only on the product of the ranges of those marginal cdfs (Wikipedia: Sklar’s theorem).







Note 5.2: ℹ️ Counts need a randomised quantile



UMI counts are discrete, so Theorem 5.1 does not give a unique copula density. scDesign2 and scDesign3 use the distributional transform

u_{cg}=(1-v_{cg})\,F_{cg}(x_{cg}-1)+v_{cg}\,F_{cg}(x_{cg}),
\qquad
v_{cg}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\mathrm{Unif}(0,1),
\tag{5.14}
which spreads each integer over its probability mass before applying \Phi^{-1}. The Gaussian copula on that scale is the dependence model of Figure 5.5. The draws v_{cg} make the copula likelihood of Section 5.5.3 random as well. Clayton, Gumbel, and t copulas are not used.




5.5.3 Goodness of fit: marginal and copula AIC and BIC
A parametric margin and a copula give a likelihood, and with it a score for parameters inferred from real cells. For cell c of type j(c) with covariates fixed, the joint density is the copula density times the marginal densities, so the log-likelihood splits (Song et al. 2024):

\ell
=\underbrace{\sum_{c=1}^{n}\log\hat c\bigl(\hat F_{c1}(x_{c1}),\ldots,\hat F_{cG}(x_{cG})\mid j(c)\bigr)}_{\ell^{\mathrm{copula}}}
+\underbrace{\sum_{c=1}^{n}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\log\hat f_{cg}(x_{cg})}_{\ell^{\mathrm{marginal}}},
\tag{5.15}

\mathrm{AIC}=2k-2\ell,
\qquad
\mathrm{BIC}=k\log n-2\ell,
\qquad
\mathrm{AIC}=\mathrm{AIC}^{\mathrm{copula}}+\mathrm{AIC}^{\mathrm{marginal}},
\tag{5.16}
and likewise for BIC, with each part counting only its own parameters. Smaller values indicate a better fit. For the Gaussian copula,

\log c(\boldsymbol{u}\mid\boldsymbol{R})
=-\tfrac12\log\det\boldsymbol{R}
-\tfrac12\,\boldsymbol{z}^{\top}\bigl(\boldsymbol{R}^{-1}-\mathbf{I}_G\bigr)\boldsymbol{z},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{z}=\Phi^{-1}(\boldsymbol{u}),
\tag{5.17}
which is finite whenever \boldsymbol{R} is positive definite. With Equation 5.12, \log\det\boldsymbol{R}=-\log\det\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j-\sum_g\log\Sigma_{gg}, so the copula likelihood of the precision-based arm costs one Cholesky factor of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j per type.
The parameter counts are

k^{\mathrm{marginal}}=2GJ\ \text{(negative binomial, mean and dispersion per gene and type)},
\qquad
k^{\mathrm{copula}}=
\begin{cases}
J\,G(G-1)/2 & \text{empirical Gaussian},\\
\sum_j\lvert E_j\rvert & \text{precision-based},\\
0 & \text{independence}.
\end{cases}

Three comparisons follow, each on the same cells and the same genes.

Margin family, gene by gene. Compare the marginal AIC or BIC of Poisson, negative binomial and zero-inflated negative binomial for each gene and type. The Poisson is the boundary \psi\to\infty of the negative binomial, where a likelihood-ratio test is not \chi^{2}_{1}; an information criterion avoids that test. Genes that the Poisson wins are the low-variability genes of a homogeneous type; a zero-inflated margin should win rarely for UMI counts.
Dependence model, margins fixed. With identical margins, \ell^{\mathrm{marginal}} cancels and only the copula part compares independence, the precision-based copula along the graphical-lasso path, and a vine. The empirical Gaussian copula drops out when G>n_j because its likelihood is not defined. For sparse precisions with G comparable to n_j, the extended BIC adds 4\gamma\lvert E_j\rvert\log G to the copula BIC (Foygel and Drton 2010), the same criterion used to choose \lambda (choosing \lambda).
Cell-type partition. For clusterings of the same cells, scDesign3’s marginal BIC tracked the adjusted Rand index with known labels (mean Spearman correlation below -0.7 across eight datasets). The copula BIC did not, because its G^{2} parameter count dominates. Merging two transcriptionally close types and comparing marginal BIC tests whether the data support the split that DeCovarT will have to resolve.

These scores are relative, and three cautions keep them honest.

Cells are not independent units. All cells come from one gastruloid experiment (Note 3.1). The \log n in BIC then overstates the information, so the ranking of models is more trustworthy than the size of the differences. A held-out log-likelihood on cells left out of the fit is a useful second check.
The copula likelihood is random for counts. It depends on the draws v_{cg} of Equation 5.14; average it over several draws, or fix the seed, before comparing models.
Margins are plugged in. The copula is fitted on uniforms from estimated margins (inference functions for margins). Its AIC and BIC ignore the uncertainty of the margins, which is another reason to read differences as rankings.



5.5.4 Generate: freeze proportions and library size
Cell types are labelled, so the synthetic sample keeps the observed composition and the observed read depths. scDesign3 draws \boldsymbol{U}_{c'} from the fitted copula and sets Y_{c'g}=\hat F_{c'g}^{-1}(U_{c'g}); changing the expected depth from N to N' multiplies the mean parameter by N'/N (Song et al. 2024). The arm uses the per-cell version of that rescaling.

Cell-type proportions stay \pi_{j}=n_{j}/n. They are not redrawn.
For each synthetic cell of type j, the library size L is taken from a real cell of that type and enters the offset of Equation 5.11, so that \sum_{g}\mathbb{E}[X_{g}]=L.
Draw the latent Gaussian \boldsymbol{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R_{j}), set u_{g}=\Phi(z_{g}), and invert the negative-binomial quantile function at (\mu_{gj},\psi_{gj}).

The synthetic matrix has the same genes, the same type proportions, and matched per-cell depth. Re-fitting \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j} on it is the recovery check for the exported precision.

text:
5.7 Perspectives

5.7.1 Two-scale optimal transport
Single-cell residual variation and variation of cell-type profiles across independent samples are different covariances. With a latent Gaussian Z for cell c of type k in sample r,

Z_{rkc}
=
\mu_{k}
+
U_{rk}
+
\varepsilon_{rkc},

U_{rk} has covariance \Sigma_{\mathrm{pop}} and \varepsilon has covariance \Sigma_{\mathrm{cell}}. The average of n cells then has covariance \Sigma_{\mathrm{pop}}+n^{-1}\Sigma_{\mathrm{cell}}, so the two precisions differ even when they share edges. Figure 5.6 draws those two networks side by side.
The regular case is an external population Gaussian Q_{R}=\mathcal{N}(\mu_{R},\Sigma_{R}), independent of the single-cell fit. Alignment is the closed-form 2-Wasserstein distance between the estimated population law \mathcal{N}(\mu_{P},\Omega_{P}^{-1}) and Q_{R},

W_{2}^{2}
=
\|\mu_{P}-\mu_{R}\|_{2}^{2}
+
\operatorname{tr}\Bigl(
\Omega_{P}^{-1}
+
\Sigma_{R}
-
2
\bigl(
\Omega_{P}^{-1/2}
\Sigma_{R}
\Omega_{P}^{-1/2}
\bigr)^{1/2}
\Bigr).
\tag{5.18}
The optimal map is affine. It moves one population Gaussian onto the other. It does not replace \Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}. A separate penalty can encourage shared edges between the cell-level and population-level precisions; that penalty is not the transport. DecOT estimates bulk proportions by an entropic transport loss between count histograms (Liu et al. 2022). That is a deconvolution competitor, not a construction of \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}.






Figure 5.6: Two regulatory scales, and Gaussian Wasserstein alignment of population profiles to an external reference.





5.7.2 scMultiSim
scMultiSim is a mechanistic multi-omics generator: a user GRN, plus chromatin, RNA velocity, space, and cell–cell interaction (Li et al. 2025). The RNA channel can emit counts from a known skeleton. The other modalities are outside this design. The default synthetic counts are the scDesign3 arm above.

title: 6  Mean-based deconvolution comparators
text:
6.1 What is being compared
DeCovarT deconvolves bulk profiles with both a mean signature and a per-type covariance. The comparators in this part do not. They estimate a composition \boldsymbol{p} from a mean signature built on the same labelled single-cell reference, and they are the baseline against which a covariance model has to move the estimate.
Three second-generation algorithms are planned on GSE229386, at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h, for the standard Wnt pulse and the early pulse (Section 2.1):
Literature keys for these three methods are not yet in bibliography/REFERENCES.bib. Add them from Zotero before a review pass; do not cite them by invented keys.
None of the three returns (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}). They are composition estimators. Sensitivity of those compositions to a misspecified precision is the last chapter of this part (Section 8.1). The early-versus-standard reading of their output is Section 7.1.
No proportions are reported here. Scripts stay eval: false until the bulk and signature objects exist.

title: 6  Mean-based deconvolution comparators
text:
BayesPrism — a Bayesian model that treats the single-cell reference as a prior on cell-type expression and updates that prior with the bulk counts.
SCDC — a weighted non-negative least-squares ensemble that can combine more than one single-cell reference. Here there is only one reference, so the ensemble weight is not a second biological replicate.
DWLS — dampened weighted least squares, which down-weights genes whose mean expression would otherwise dominate the fit.

title: 7  Early versus standard Wnt
text:
7.1 Compositional reading
Second-generation mean-based deconvolution (BayesPrism, SCDC, DWLS; Section 6.1) on the bulk series is a compositional narrative, not DeCovarT’s covariance model. Figure 7.1 contrasts a standard Wnt pulse at 48 h with a premature pulse at 24 h, at the three bulk-matched times.
On the control-like arm, 72 h is primitive-streak enriched and 96 h shows pre-somitic mesoderm and somite progression. On the early Wnt arm, 48 h retains more naïve pluripotency, 72 h is dominated by ectopic pluripotency with a reduced primitive streak, and 96 h nearly loses pre-somitic mesoderm. Absolute abundances disagree across algorithms — weighted least squares is sensitive to collinearity among neighbouring states — so we treat direction of change (ectopic pluripotency up, primitive streak and pre-somitic mesoderm down) as the consensus, not the point estimates.
That reading is why GRNs are fit per type and per time at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h (Section 2.1): those are the slots where a bulk composition exists to confront the Gaussians. Cell line remains out of the precision model.
